Korean Memory Giants Cautious on 3D ICs as China’s CXMT Accelerates Niche Strategy

The race to improve AI semiconductor performance is shifting away from process-node miniaturization and toward advanced stacking technologies that vertically integrate chips. This comes as 3D integrated circuits, which combine logic and memory in a single package, emerge as a key technology for next-generation AI semiconductors. With rising demand not only for general-purpose AI chips led by Nvidia but also for application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) and inference chips, efforts to integrate memory and logic according to individual customer requirements are also gaining momentum.

According to semiconductor industry sources on the 24th, global fabless companies and AI chipmakers have recently been actively exploring the adoption of 3D IC technology. Samsung Electronics’ foundry business, in particular, is reportedly receiving a steady stream of related inquiries.

“When we ask Samsung’s foundry division about 3D ICs, we are told that virtually every prospective customer these days is asking about the technology,” said an official from the fabless industry. “Interest is growing rapidly as it coincides with demand for differentiated AI chips.”

Industry officials, however, say the emerging 3D IC market has a fundamentally different business structure from the conventional DRAM industry. DRAM-based 3D ICs, in particular, are essentially a form of custom DRAM designed to meet specific customer requirements, making them distinct from the traditional memory business of mass-producing standardized products.

“3D DRAM can ultimately be viewed as customized DRAM,” a semiconductor industry official said. “Each customer requires a different memory configuration and stacking method, so it is fundamentally different from a business that mass-produces standardized products.”

“Samsung Electronics and SK hynix base their core business models on the mass production of standard DRAM,” the official continued. “Producing customized DRAM exclusively for individual customers may not be economically viable for them.”

The industry therefore expects Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to continue preliminary research into 3D IC technology while remaining cautious about full-scale commercialization. Although research and development or new-business reviews are possible, the prevailing view is that it will be difficult for such efforts to expand to the point of mobilizing entire business divisions.

For this reason, industry watchers believe that later entrants targeting niche markets, rather than large-scale mass production, may be the first to pursue the 3D IC market.

China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is a prominent example.

With U.S. semiconductor restrictions on China making it difficult for CXMT to enter the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) market, the company is reportedly working to secure capabilities in 3D ICs as one of the next-generation AI memory technologies. Analysts say CXMT has chosen to target the custom memory market instead of competing head-on with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix in commodity DRAM.

“China has already produced a number of 3D DRAM sample chips ahead of the rest of the world, and we are also working on several related projects,” another semiconductor industry official said. “Going forward, companies such as CXMT and Winbond that target niche markets are likely to be the first to establish the market.”

items.title: I’d like to share an interesting anecdote related to this. In 2007, AMD established a major research and development center in Shanghai, China. The company believed it needed Chinese engineers to compete with NVIDIA. After careful consideration, AMD decided to foster internal competition by pitting a Chinese team against an American team within its Shanghai operation. The initiative was called the “Saima” (賽馬, literally “horse racing”) Project. Saima is an extreme internal competition system in which several teams are assigned the same project, with only the best-performing team’s work ultimately selected. The result? The Chinese team far outperformed the American team in R&D efficiency.

items.title: •MI500 brings optical interconnects, ahead of Nvidia Rubin Ultra in key areas (HBM, 4-die package, scale-up domain). 👀
items.content:
•MI500 brings optical interconnects, ahead of Nvidia Rubin Ultra in key areas (HBM, 4-die package, scale-up domain).

👀Jeff Pu (@sssjeffpu)AMD AI Takeaways Note

•AI accelerator market now seen at $1.4T by 2030 (up from $1T prior). We also raises forecast to $1T by 2028, backed by our bottom-up analysis 
•Server CPU TAM also boosted to >$220B by 2030. Agentic AI expected to be ~50% of TAM, with CPU:GPU ratio tightening toward 1:1.
•MI455X is a major leap: 34x higher throughput & 18x lower token cost vs MI355X. Already outperforming Nvidia B200 in some LLM inference.
•MI500 brings optical interconnects, ahead of Nvidia Rubin Ultra in key areas (HBM, 4-die package, scale-up domain).
•Venice CPU strongest for AI workloads: 2.2x/2.0x higher throughput vs competitors. We estimate ~300k CoWoS builds expected in 2027 → big ASP uplift. 
📈 No change to estimates and TP
